messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Mariana had spent three decades as a detective, but nothing prepared her for the call that Saturday evening—a clandestine drug lab explosion in a warehouse on the south side. She arrived before the hazmat team, pushing through a crowd of panicked neighbors to reach a collapsed wall. A cloud of acrid fumes hit her as she knelt to check for survivors; her lungs seized, and she gasped, tasting something metallic and chemical. She felt her own sweat pooling under her vest, the sour smell mixing with the burning plastic. A paramedic later guided her to an ambulance, where the sterile antiseptic and latex gloves burned into her memory. That night in the emergency room, the doctors told her the chemicals were unstable but she would recover. Mariana did breathe again, but not the way she used to.

In the weeks that followed, she found herself ducking into doorways whenever she heard a sudden bang—a truck backfiring, a dropped metal tray in the precinct break room. Her body stayed tense, her shoulders knotted, her eyes darting across the parking lot before she got out of her car. What frightened her most was the way the hospital smell would catch her off guard. The first time she walked past a clinic, her throat tightened, and she had to cover her face with both hands, forcing herself to think of the grocery list instead. Even a colleague’s sweat after a morning run made her stomach drop and her mind leap back to that warehouse floor, but only in jagged pieces—a flash of a chemical drum, the paramedic’s glove, the cold oxygen mask—never the whole thing. She had come to believe that she would never feel normal emotions again, that her body would always be this coiled, that the department that sent her in without proper gear had failed her entirely. That last belief made her flinch every time she saw a uniform, so she started avoiding the squad room, taking paperwork home, speaking only to her partner through text.

The connections tightened into a loop she could not name. A sudden sound put her on high alert and, at the same time, shoved a fragmented memory into her throat; she blocked it before it finished, and the very act of blocking convinced her she was losing control of her own mind. The more she believed she had to be on guard all the time, the more she scanned the hallway for shadows, and the more she scanned, the more breathless she became when she caught the faintest hint of a cleaning product. That breathlessness sent her straight to her old redirection trick—picturing her daughter’s graduation—but the trick also reinforced her sense that the memory was too dangerous to face. She had started hiding her face at her desk whenever a nurse’s perfume drifted by, and in those moments the event felt present again, not over. Each time she pushed the memory away, the negative appraisal that she was permanently broken grew stronger, and that appraisal made her avoid not only smells but also authority figures: she no longer attended briefings with the captain, citing a stomach bug. Her work suffered—she missed a deadline on a burglary case—and her partner gently asked if she was okay. She said she was fine, but she was certain she was not.

What finally brought Mariana to seek help was a piece of evidence: a forensic photo from a new case, a chemical spill at a manufacturing plant. The image alone triggered a surge of breathlessness so intense she thought she would black out. She drove herself to the precinct’s employee assistance office, her hands shaking on the wheel. What she hoped for was to stop the loop—to be able to walk into the break room without covering her face, to hear a door slam without her heart racing. But what she feared most was that the loop would not break, that the institutional failure she blamed would never be fixed, and that the woman who used to lead scenes would remain fractured, always on guard, always bracing for a trigger she could not predict.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers directly cause negative appraisals; triggers cause memory, threat, or maladaptive strategies, but not appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause memory; negative appraisals are consequences of strategies or memory, not vice versa.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause triggers; appraisals may influence perception but not cause the external triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies directly cause memory; strategies are used to suppress or avoid memory, not to produce it.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even a colleague's sweat after a morning run made her stomach drop and her mind leap back to that warehouse floor, but only in jagged pieces—a flash of a chemical drum, the paramedic's glove, the cold oxygen mask—never the whole thing.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time a trigger struck like that, it drove the conviction deeper that she would never feel normal again and that her body was permanently wired for alarm.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She had come to believe that she would never feel normal emotions again, that her body would always be this coiled, that the department that sent her in without proper gear had failed her entirely.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That belief kept her tethered to the explosion scene, as if her mind needed to revisit the exact moment where normal ended, so the memory stayed close and vivid.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She had come to believe that she would never feel normal emotions again, that her body would always be this coiled, that the department that sent her in without proper gear had failed her entirely.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once she was convinced that the world and her own body were no longer safe, nearly every ordinary sound or smell became a trigger — a car backfiring, a whiff of bleach, a colleague's aftershave — because her appraisals had turned the everyday into a landscape of potential threats.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She blocked it before it finished, and the very act of blocking convinced her she was losing control of her own mind.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But that blocking had the unintended effect of keeping the memory intact and unprocessed, so that when it next surfaced it arrived with a force she could not counter — all that suppression had preserved it in full.
<<<END>>>
